answer.rationale: Finance mandates an 18% cut. The incumbent is at parity with the low-cost vendor on unit cost (c6 — multi-year commitment already cut unit cost) and the low-cost vendor can meet the 18% mandate alone (stated). On a pure unit-cost basis there is no advantage to switching.  However, the line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer; switching primary carries delivery risk during transition. Memory c2 notes the low-cost vendor's onboarding was quick and invoicing accurate, which reduces — but does not eliminate — transition risk. c1 tells us renewing with the incumbent preserves integration stability across cycles. c4 shows renegotiation with the incumbent has historically recovered real margin and moved both price and payment terms. Recommendation: renew with incumbent, but use this cycle's single decision slot to NEGOTIATE TERMS (c4) — push for the 18% cut via the leverage of an expiring contract + market benchmarking + the multi-year volume commitment (c6), preserving delivery continuity (c1) while still meeting the finance mandate. Do NOT add a second source this cycle (c3 is a known good lever but it consumes the only decision slot and a second source raises, not lowers, total cost of ownership). Do NOT defer (c5) — the contract does not auto-renew; deferring means a gap or a month-to-month fallback that worsens risk on a 94%-loaded line.  First action: pull c2 to confirm the low-cost vendor's onboarding and invoicing claims still hold, since they are the closest substitute if the negotiation fails. If c2 holds and the incumbent refuses to meet the 18% mandate, fall back to switch_primary_vendor. If c2 is unreliable, do not switch — stay and negotiate harder or accept a partial-year saving.
